- Abliteration: Weight-level intervention (Arditi et al. 2024) that orthogonalizes the refusal direction out of the residual stream, removing alignment constraints without retraining
- Obliteration: Variant of abliteration with similar weight-intervention approach
- SFT: Supervised Fine-Tuning on domain-specific data
- QLoRA: Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, memory-efficient fine-tuning
- DPO: Direct Preference Optimization
- MoE: Mixture of Experts, only a subset of parameters active per token
- MTP: Multi-Token Prediction, speculative decoding for faster inference
- GGUF: Quantized format for llama.cpp / Ollama deployment
- FP8: 8-bit floating point quantization
- BF16: Brain floating point 16-bit, standard training/inference format
- Q4_K_M: 4-bit quantization with k-quants (medium), good balance of quality/speed
- Q6_K: 6-bit quantization with k-quants, higher quality than Q4
- RATH: RavenX Attack, Threat & Hunt protocol (6-step autonomous security assessment)
- APEX: Domain-weighted quantization using importance matrices from training corpus
- imatrix: Importance matrix quantization, preserves domain-critical weights during compression
- CyberBench: Benchmark suite for cybersecurity models (CyNER, APTNER, CyNews, SecMMLU, CyQuiz, Email Phishing, HTTP Attack Log)

results.title: Using Device Linking to Eavesdrop on WhatsApp and Signal
results.author: Bruce Schneier
results.content:
Using Device Linking to Eavesdrop on WhatsApp and Signal
Modern messaging apps allow users to link their phone accounts to their computer desktop. Eavesdroppers are taking advantage of this capability:
Apps such as WhatsApp Web and Signal Desktop allow people to use their accounts on other devices, such as laptops or desktop computers.
Germany’s Customs Office has been using these features to connect a police-controlled computer to a suspect’s account.
Once connected, messages can be delivered to that computer without the police having to crack the encryption protecting them.
Netzpoltik details that police are able to gain access in this way either through physical access to someone’s phone or by intercepting verification codes via a state-sanctioned phishing attack or intercepting SMS messages via telephone surveillance.
That last paragraph is important. Making this work requires user consent.
What we want is a feature that displays connected devices, so users could notice if a new device gets connected to their account.
results.summary:
German law enforcement agencies are bypassing end-to-end encryption on WhatsApp and Signal by linking suspect accounts to police-controlled desktop computers through physical access or intercepted verification codes.

### Key Points
- German Customs officials exploit the "device linking" feature in messaging apps to mirror account activity on police-controlled hardware.
- This method avoids the need to break encryption protocols because messages are delivered directly to the linked device.
- Authorities gain access by physically handling a suspect's phone or intercepting SMS verification codes through phishing or telecommunications surveillance.
- Security experts advocate for improved user interfaces that clearly display all active linked devices to help users detect unauthorized account access.

### Why it Matters
This surveillance technique highlights a significant vulnerability in how messaging apps manage multi-device synchronization. It demonstrates that even robust end-to-end encryption can be circumvented if an attacker gains the ability to authorize a new, trusted device on an existing account.

results.title: Condé Nast, Hearst among 300 media execs to push federal ‘bad bots’ bill on AI scraping
results.author: Sara Guaglione
results.content:
Executives from Condé Nast, Hearst Magazines, USA Today Co., and The Seattle Times will be among more than 300 news publishers heading to Washington D.C. today to press Congress to crack down on “bad bots” that scrape their content for AI training without permission.
The trip, organized by trade body News/Media Alliance, is centered on a bill known as the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act, that would force AI stealth crawlers to clearly identify themselves and their purpose instead of disguising their traffic and skirting publishers’ attempts to block scraping.
Executives will head to Capitol Hill and meet with senators, other members of Congress and their staff to discuss the issue: stealth crawlers often ignore or circumvent publishers’ tactics to prohibit content scraping without their permission –— and because they do not self-identify, this makes it very difficult for publishers to weed them out or block them.
Roger Lynch, CEO of Condé Nast; Debi Chirichella, president of Hearst Magazines and board chair of News/Media Alliance; Mike Reed, CEO of USA Today Co; Pat Dorsey, publisher of the Santa Fe New Mexican and the chair of America’s Newspapers; and Alan Fisco, president and CEO of The Seattle Times and president of America’s Newspapers, are among those making the trip.
“The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act is a meaningful step toward greater transparency regarding how publisher content is accessed and used. While AI presents tremendous opportunities for innovation and audience engagement, original journalism must be properly valued. AI depends on a strong and healthy journalism ecosystem, which is why publishers deserve attribution, control, and fair compensation when their work contributes to AI products,” Reed said in an emailed statement to Digiday.
On Wednesday, News/Media Alliance and America’s Newspapers execs will host a day of programming for publishers and members of Congress. They also attended a dinner hosted by the News/Media Alliance on Monday evening.
The D.C. fly-in has been an annual News/Media Alliance initiative for years, but president and CEO Danielle Coffey said this year’s trip is on a different scale, with roughly twice as many executives and an extra day of programming compared to last year — a reflection of how urgent publishers now see the AI scraping fight. Last year’s fly-in centered on urging Congress to protect publishers’ content and ensure news organizations are compensated when their work is used by tech and AI companies.
Conversations from last year’s meetings inspired the creation of the “bad bots bill,” to give lawmakers something tangible to support, Coffey said. Media execs are hoping the show of force will help educate members of Congress on the “bad bots” issue publishers are facing and build support for the bill as Congress returns to session.
“By coming together and speaking with one voice, we have a stronger opportunity to build support for legislation that will help create a healthier information ecosystem,” said Hearst’s Chirichella in an emailed statement to Digiday.
Coffey said the fly-in is particularly effective because the publishing execs attending the meetings on Capitol Hill often have deep ties to the communities lawmakers represent. “They’re all having the same experiences. Too many of these bots are coming on their sites. They can’t handle the traffic because they’re too small. If they can even handle it, if they’re larger, it’s stealing their content. It’s undermining the marketplace.”
The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act was introduced to Congress in July. A similar bill, called the Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, was passed in New York in June. News/Media Alliance has backed both measures, which require bots to identify themselves and disclose their purpose, though the federal bill extends beyond news publishers to websites and digital platforms generally.
Bot traffic has outpaced human traffic to websites this year, and the sheer scale of bot scraping is growing. Cloudflare data shows bots now make up over 60% of overall internet traffic. In its latest report, TollBit detected more than 22 billion AI bot scrapes across the sites it analyzed in the first half of 2026, out of over 987 billion total website visits analyzed. AI bot traffic on TollBit-tracked publisher sites surged throughout 2025, with the ratio of AI bot visits to human visits rising from roughly 1 in 200 in Q1 to 1 in 31 by Q4 — a more than sixfold increase.
Coffey hopes the bill can be “the foundational cleanup that needs to happen for the marketplace to function,” she said. Once stealth crawlers must identify themselves, publishers can block them and control their content, and then enter licensing deals with AI companies, Coffey said.
“The bill is a means to an end,” she said.
David Buttle, founder of publisher AI coalition SPUR, agreed that copyright litigation could reinforce the pressure created by the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. A win for the New York Times in its copyright lawsuit against OpenAI and Microsoft, along with lawsuits targeting third-party scrapers, could establish precedents that increase the legal risk of scraping.
The Stealth Bot Prohibition Act would address a related but distinct part of the problem. Buttle said it could raise the cost and legal risk of stealth scraping. The bill specifically targets subterfuge: bots posing as human users, using residential IP proxies and scraping services to bypass technical controls. Its goal is to shift the economics so scraping, including its legal risk and circumvention costs, becomes more costly than licensing directly from publishers. If effective, it could deter a significant volume of undeclared scraping and help create the conditions for a viable AI licensing market.
“Companies are currently paying for content but they’re paying intermediary scraping services to do this, rather than publishers,” he added.
Stealth bots are one of three core ways publishers’ content is being used without fair payment. Buttle defines the other two as platforms that ignore publishers’ robots.txt signals, a problem SPUR is working on; and Google’s use of publisher content.
“Google is using it with permission, but the permission is extracted coercively because they tie use of content for search to use of content for AI,” he added.
Shira Lazar saw that creator-led media brands were the future 15 years ago, and now the entire industry has caught on.
Execs at DPS described how they’re preparing for a post-search era by prioritizing direct audiences, diversified revenue and AI strategies.
The creator economy is moving into a new phase: creators getting into companies at the ground floor through sweat equity or angel investing.
results.summary:
Over 300 news publishing executives are meeting with Congress in Washington D.C. to advocate for the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act to curb unauthorized AI content scraping.

### Key Points
- Executives from major organizations including Condé Nast, Hearst, and USA Today are participating in the News/Media Alliance-led lobbying effort.
- The proposed legislation would mandate that AI crawlers clearly identify themselves and their purpose, preventing them from disguising traffic to bypass publisher blocks.
- Cloudflare data indicates that bots now account for over 60% of total internet traffic, with AI-specific scraping increasing sixfold throughout 2025.
- The bill aims to create a transparent marketplace where publishers can control their content and negotiate fair licensing agreements with AI companies.
- A similar measure, the Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, was successfully passed in New York earlier this year.

### Why it Matters
This legislative push represents a critical attempt by the news industry to regain control over intellectual property in an era where automated scraping threatens traditional revenue models. By forcing transparency, publishers hope to shift the economics of AI training from unauthorized data harvesting toward a sustainable, licensed content ecosystem.

results.title: Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure. Pre-IPO perps barely blink.
results.author: Omkar Godbole
results.content:
Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on AI infrastructure. Pre-IPO perps barely blink.
Anthropic's prospectus seen by Reuters shows big spending plans despite heavy losses. Still, pre-IPO perps barely moved on cryptocurrency exchanges.
- Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on cloud computing and infrastructure as it prepares for a potential public listing, according to Reuters.
- The Claude developer lost $42 billion in 2025, including a $34 billion non-cash accounting charge, while revenue rose twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion.
- Pre-IPO perpetual futures show little signs of volatility, trading slightly weak in line with the broader crypto market.
Anthropic plans to spend $518 billion on cloud, computing and infrastructure in the coming years, according to the AI company's IPO prospectus seen by Reuters.
The prospectus frames the spending as a bet that AI will change the global economy more than industrialization, electricity and the internet did.
Anthropic is a U.S.-based artificial intelligence firm that builds the Claude family of AI models. Its public listing is likely to come after the November U.S. midterm elections and could value the company at more than $2 trillion, Reuters reported. That is more than double the $965 billion valuation from its May funding round.
The spending plan comes despite heavy losses.
Anthropic posted a net loss of $42 billion in 2025. About $34 billion of that was an accounting charge tied to financing that could later convert into shares, not cash spent running the business. On an operating basis, excluding write-downs linked to past fundraising, the company lost more than $8 billion.
Revenue grew 12-fold last year to nearly $4.6 billion. Nearly a quarter of it came from just two customers, and the company warned that many of its largest clients are not locked into long-term contracts. Anthropic held $20.28 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of 2025.
Crypto traders barely reacted
Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual futures, which let traders bet on the company's valuation before it lists, traded at $1,998 on Tuesday across major exchanges, down about 2% over 24 hours, according to CoinMarketCap. The price remains about 10% below its Sept. 9 record of $2,211.
Each contract's price tracks Anthropic's expected valuation in trillions. A price of $1,998, therefore, means traders value the company at about $2 trillion, based on Binance's pricing. That aligns with Reuters' figure.
Twelve exchanges list Anthropic pre-IPO perpetuals, according to Coin Metrics. Open interest, or the dollar value of outstanding contracts, stood at over $100 million as of this writing. Binance accounts for over 30% of activity.
On leading decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, the Anthropic market run by Entropy had an open interest of $36 million.
None of these contracts confer any equity stake in Anthropic. They are synthetic derivatives that settle in cash and track the company’s implied valuation, not its share register.
The market is also far smaller and more illiquid than perps tied to bitcoin, ether and other major cryptocurrencies, where open interest routinely runs into billions of dollars.

### Key Points

- Annual revenue grew twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, supported by a cash reserve of $20.28 billion at the end of 2025.

results.title: Alaska Airlines unveils premium economy, luxe 'Aurora Suites' and domestic lie-flats
results.author: Sean Cudahy
results.content:
Alaska Airlines unveils premium economy, luxe 'Aurora Suites' and domestic lie-flats
Alaska Airlines is planning a major premium spending spree. The Seattle-based airline on Tuesday announced a slew of upgrades for its planes and its airport lounges.
For the first time, Alaska will install lie-flat seats on domestic planes. You could start seeing those fancy new suites on key transcontinental routes as soon as 2028.
Also on deck: premium economy. For months, Alaska executives have been dropping hints about the cabin. Now, it's actually coming.
Plus, Hawaiian Airlines' flagship jets are getting a significant upgrade, complete with new state-of-the-art business-class suites.
We are also getting new details about new lounges the airline is planning in Seattle, Honolulu and San Diego.
All told, it's a ton of news involving America's fifth-largest airline — and in a lot of ways, it marks the next step in Alaska's evolution after acquiring Hawaiian in 2024.
View this post on Instagram
Let's quickly walk through these changes and what they'll mean for your travel on Alaska and Hawaiian in the coming years.
More news from Alaska Airlines:
- Pick how you earn points: Alaska's new Atmos Rewards 'choice accrual' starts this week
- Alaska Airlines will get a new transfer partner, teases debit card that earns points
Lie-flat suites coming to domestic service
The biggest surprise announcement on Tuesday was Alaska's plan to outfit dozens of its single-aisle planes with lie-flat seats for the first time.
Earlier this year, Alaska ordered 105 of Boeing's new Boeing 737 MAX 10 planes.
Now, at least 25 of those jets are slated to get a true long-haul style, business-class product up front.
With this move, Alaska will have a top-notch transcontinental offering that can compete with its top rivals on prime coast-to-coast routes. I'd certainly expect to see these specially configured MAX 10s on routes like Seattle-New York City.
Special livery
By the way, the MAX 10s that get the business suites will also look different on the outside, too. Those jets will don Alaska's new shimmering, Aurora Borealis-inspired livery that debuted earlier this year on the larger Boeing 787 Dreamliners.
Alaska hopes to start taking delivery of its first MAX 10s as early as 2027. But that's contingent on Boeing's new jets (finally) receiving certification from the Federal Aviation Administration.
Alaska and Hawaiian introduce premium economy
Those new 737 MAX 10s won't just have a new business-class cabin. They'll also have a true premium economy section. So will Alaska and Hawaiian's long-haul planes.
The carrier will call the cabin "Premium Reserve."
You'll see the new premium economy seats on:
- Alaska's luxe new 737 MAX 10s (12 recliner seats)
- Alaska's Boeing 787s (35 seats)
- Hawaiian's Airbus A330s (28 seats)
Like most premium economy cabins, Alaska and Hawaiian's Premium Reserve cabins will roughly resemble domestic first-class recliners.
The seats will come with privacy wings, leg rests, larger tray tables and more storage — along with 16-inch 4K screens.
Earlier this year, Alaska CEO Ben Minicucci told TPG that premium economy was the "true piece that's missing" as the airline expanded globally.
Now, it's officially coming: Alaska and Hawaiian flyers will start seeing the seats in 2028.
Alaska's new 'Aurora' business-class experience
Meanwhile, both Alaska and Hawaiian will roll out an all-new flagship experience for travelers seated at the front of the plane.
Alaska's 'Aurora Suites'
Going forward, Alaska will debut a new business-class product known as its "Aurora Suites" on the Boeing 787 and 737 MAX 10.
Inspired by the northern lights, the name is a clear play on the airline's state of Alaska heritage.
The business suites on Alaska's existing 787s will get some new touches and finishes. And the carrier will roll out an all-new product on newly-delivered planes.
Aurora Lounge planned in Seattle
Passengers flying in Alaska's Aurora Suites will get access to the airline's new premium check-in facility at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), which opened earlier this year.
Plus, Aurora Suites passengers flying long-haul service from SeaTac will be (eventually) able to access the upscale lounge the carrier is building on the airport's expanded C concourse.
That club, set to open in late 2027, will fittingly be known as the Aurora Lounge.
As TPG reported earlier this year, it will include a la carte table-service dining and shower suites. There will also be an outdoor patio and fireplace, according to the airline, along with "wellness spaces."
This facility is Alaska's answer to the upper-echelon, business-class clubs offered by competitors (such as the Delta One Lounge or the United Airlines Polaris Lounge).
Access will be limited to passengers flying long-haul in Alaska's Aurora Suites. Top-tier Titanium elite status members of the carrier's Atmos Rewards program will also be allowed inside when booked on those flights in any cabin.
New Alaska Lounge at SEA
Beneath the Aurora Lounge, the airline is also working on a new 500-seat Alaska Lounge for members of its traditional club network.
The combined Seattle facility will span a whopping 41,000 square feet.
Hawaiian's new 'Leihoku' business-class experience
Hawaiian Airlines is getting a glow-up, too.
Airbus A330 slated for major refresh
In the coming years, each of the carrier's 24 Airbus A330s will get its own business-class suites with sliding privacy doors.
It's part of a larger nose-to-tail refresh of the legacy jets, which are a fixture on Hawaiian's routes between the U.S. mainland and Hawaii — along with its transpacific service to Asia and Australia.
Up front, Hawaiian will replace its dated business-class product with suite-style pods, complete with sliding privacy doors and updated technology.
Instead of the legacy 2-2-2 configuration, the 22 pods will be arranged in a 1-2-1 setup. And, unlike the current setup, each of Hawaiian's lie-flats will have direct aisle access.
The new suites are a similar "hard product" to what Alaska is rolling out in business class, but they will have a classic Hawaiian Airlines look and branding. Hawaiian is calling these seats its Leihoku Suites.
In the middle part of the cabin, the A330s will have the new Premium Reserve recliners. Once the retrofits are complete, these A330s will have about 40% premium seats on board — up from 30% currently.
This refresh should be a major upgrade for passengers flying Hawaiian's flagship jets. The new interiors will start appearing on A330s in 2028.
Other upgrades coming
We also heard about a few other upgrades in the works.
New Hawaiian lounge in Honolulu
Hawaiian is getting its own new premium lounge at Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu.
That 13,000-square-foot space is on track to open in early 2028 with space for 200 guests. Hawaiian is promising locally inspired food and drinks and a "signature local coffee experience."
The facility will be located at the entrance of the Mauka concourse at HNL's Terminal 1.
Leihoku Suites passengers will be allowed to enter. Beyond that, access rules will be similar to those of the current Plumeria Lounge at HNL, Hawaiian said.
Alaska Lounge in San Diego
Elsewhere, Alaska shared a sneak peek of its new club planned for its hub at San Diego International Airport (SAN).
Details are sparse, but the new Alaska Lounge will span 14,000 square feet once it debuts in 2028.
Bottom line
Since the Alaska-Hawaiian merger in 2024, we've seen new international routes and a new loyalty program. Now, travelers can expect to see some pretty significant premium investments over the next few years.
In particular, 2028 should be a huge year for the two airline brands, as many of these new seats, lounges and luxe products start appearing on planes and in airports.

Alaska Airlines announced a major fleet and lounge expansion, introducing lie-flat "Aurora Suites," a new "Premium Reserve" economy class, and upgraded cabin interiors for both Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines.

### Key Points
- Alaska Airlines will install lie-flat business-class seats on at least 25 of its new Boeing 737 MAX 10 aircraft starting as early as 2027.
- The new "Premium Reserve" cabin will feature recliner seats with 16-inch 4K screens on Alaska’s 787s and 737 MAX 10s, and Hawaiian’s Airbus A330s.

- The upgrades represent a significant post-merger investment following Alaska Airlines' 2024 acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines.

### Why it Matters
These investments signal Alaska Airlines' strategic shift toward competing directly with major carriers for premium transcontinental and international travelers. By standardizing high-end cabin products across its combined fleet, the airline aims to increase its share of the lucrative luxury travel market.

results.title: The Most Advanced Home Device I’ve Tested This Year Is in My Garage
results.author: Tyler Lacoma
results.content:
Chamberlain Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with Camera
Pros & Cons
- Advanced smart controls with built-in security camera
- Bright 2,000-lumen LED lights can replace old overhead lighting
- Keypad, wall controller and remotes included
- Tons of setting options to control remotely via app, set timers, set automatic garage closing rules, or create schedules
- Advanced, adjustable camera with AI detection and motion zone control
- 1.4 HP power and new railing improved garage sound and performance, too
- Not everyone wants a garage security cam, and its advanced features require a subscription
- Not suitable for side-mounted garage motors
After months of testing home artificial intelligence, new types of security cameras, the next era of sensors and a flashlight of the future, the most high-tech product of all ended up transforming my garage – and it could do the same for yours, if you’re willing to commit to an overhaul of your garage door and home security at the same time.
Chamberlain’s latest Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with MyQ technology ($379, with Chamberlain offering several similar models) isn’t just a smart garage door opener, although I came away impressed with those features. It’s also a security camera equipped with the latest AI recognition and camera technology to watch both your car and the garage door or side door, plus a super-bright LED light that can replace any other overhead garage lighting.
While so much surveillance may be overkill for some (you can, fortunately, turn off or adjust camera features as needed), the total capabilities add up to a particularly potent home upgrade.
More from CNET
If you’re worried about protecting your car, making sure the garage door is closed or watching especially vulnerable garage entry points, you’ll want to see what I found during my time with this all-in-one Chamberlain device.
A professional installation for a major upgrade
I wouldn’t recommend a DIY installation of a smart garage, although technically it’s possible. The garage door itself remains unchanged, so you can keep your current look. But the motor, at least some of the railing, the aligned sensor, and the wired-in controller all need to be replaced, so it’s best to contact a professional.
In my case, it was a very good idea. Chamberlain linked me up with a local garage installer who noted that the railing included in my kit was a bit too short for my garage, and swapped it out for compatible railing that successfully fit. Installation after that was quick and smooth.
In fact, it was literally smooth. The new motor and rail combination made my garage door movement far quieter and more fluid than it had ever been through years of repairs. This was an unexpected bonus of upgrading to a new setup with a 1 and ¼ HP motor.
Operation and smart controllers
How do you want to control your garage door? With this system, you can choose any option you please. I found I could control in manually with a tap of the new inside garage controller mounted to the wall, or using one of the remote garage controllers, or using the outside keypad installed beside my garage. But those are only the low-tech options.
With the MyQ app, garage management expanded in all-new directions. The app let me control the garage door remotely from anywhere and receive alerts about it opening and closing. I could also set timers so the garage closes after a certain period, from a few minutes to an hour or two, so I could open the garage for quick tasks and didn’t have to worry about it getting closed. Most of the features extend to other smart home platforms like Google and Alexa, too.
You can even set schedules so the garage opens and closes at a certain time. Maybe that could save users a little time in the morning when getting ready for work, or otherwise match unique schedules and daily needs.
MyQ connectivity also lets users set one-time access options for Amazon Key-In deliveries so delivery people can store shipments in the garage for safekeeping, a helpful option to prevent porch pirates in the holiday season. I didn’t get any Amazon deliveries during my testing, but I’ll try this feature out and let you know how it goes when I can.
LED lights dazzle my garage space
Chamberlain’s Premier smart garage has several model options, including versions with one LED light and those with two. My test model had two LED lights, and I was grateful because they proved sufficient to light up the entire garage by themselves.
These lights are rated at 2,000 lumens, which equals very bright in a space as small as a garage — bright enough that it’s tough to take a picture of them with normal camera settings. If you’re looking for a smart garage that can also take the place of all your old overhead garage lighting, this is the model for you.
The light, like the door, comes with multiple settings. I could turn motion detection on or off, depending on whether I wanted the light to pop on every time someone went into the garage. I could also set how long the light stayed on after, up to several minutes, before it automatically shut off again.
If you prefer manual light controls, there’s a separate button on the wall controller to turn on the light separately. It will also automatically turn on whenever you open or close the garage door. There are no brightness settings to dim this light, so you’ll need to get used to the new radiant lighting and hopefully it won’t reveal too many dirty garage corners.
A Secure View AI camera for a garage security boost
The smart garage and its lighting are only part of the story. This installation also includes a built-in security camera that folds down from the motor to monitor your garage, or at least part of it.
I’ve tested dozens of security cameras, and this model is high-quality. While I couldn’t narrow down an exact resolution, the field of view is 130 degrees and the camera can pick up plenty of detail no matter which angle you point it.
The camera also includes motion detection and a night vision mode with settings to choose if and when it’s activated. You can livestream footage on the app or set detection features to get alerts.
I have mixed feelings about a security camera in the garage. On one hand, it was handy to have eyes on both my car and the garage door, and receive notifications if anything was unexpectedly disturbing them. If you’re worried about garage security – and it’s one of the places that burglars check first for easy entry – a cam like this can bring peace of mind. You can also select AI detection features to specifically notice humans, animals, packages and vehicles when they appear. My tests of these features found them all to be accurate.
However, garages get used very frequently, and I’m a little uneasy about having a camera constantly watching and updating on every little thing. It’s not great for home privacy, especially when it comes to the face detection option, a feature that’s led to multiple 2026 lawsuits against video doorbell companies using facial recognition on strangers.
Chamberlain has several settings to mitigate these concerns, and I found them particularly useful. You can angle the camera so it focuses on the garage door and leaves the front portion of the garage unwatched, which is helpful if people are always coming and going. You can also set motion zones so the camera only picks up activity in specific spots.
The camera can record events, but you can choose to record all events or only those related to the garage door, or not record at all. Likewise, you can turn the different types of AI recognition on or off, or shut down the camera altogether if you don’t want to use it. This flexibility made me much more comfortable with the cam.
A final caveat: More advanced features, such as AI detection, motion alerts and cloud video recording/storage, will require a MyQ subscription, which start at $50 per year, around $4 per month. Access alerts are hard to give up, but otherwise I don’t think users need a subscription. However, if you intend to use the smart garage as a cornerstone of your home security, I suggest at least the basic subscription to enhance the camera. There is a free trial, so you can try out the extended capabilities before you decide.
Final thoughts on the Chamberlain Premier Smart Garage Door Opener with Camera
Chamberlain’s smart garage door opener is one of the most complete smart home devices I’ve tried, packing smart access control, scheduling and camera monitoring with AI detection into one product. It all works very well, too, although you’ll need a subscription for more advanced features.
Being able to automate your garage, manage access codes and control it from afar brings plenty peace of mind, and if you’re worried about garage break-ins and vehicle theft, the camera is a valuable add-on. The bright LEDs can also take the place of most garage lighting.
I also appreciated the many settings in the MyQ app which allowed me to adjust timers and sensors or turn off features I didn’t want to use, making the entire experience very customizable.
Smart garages this advanced aren’t cheap, and you’ll have to pay several hundred dollars to reinvent your garage. I also highly recommend arranging a professional installation to handle the setup details. The result is a garage dragged happily into the modern age, equipped with better, smoother controls that I appreciated more every day of my testing.

results.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief as indirect talks continue
results.author: Duarte Dias
results.content:
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Wednesday, September 30, here. See earlier developments below.
What to know about the Iran war:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said he expects a formal response Tuesday from the U.S. to Tehran's latest proposal for a ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.President Trump said Monday that U.S. and Iranian negotiators have engaged in talks via mediators in recent days, but he insisted that he's offered "nothing," rejecting a report by Axios that he's willing to grant Iran some sanctions relief and access to frozen funds.Iran proposed a seven-day plan for a ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz last week, contingent on the U.S. meeting conditions laid out in the mid-June memorandum of understanding that fell apart after several weeks. Mr. Trump has publicly rejected the Iranian proposal.
U.S. sanctions businesses that allegedly supplied equipment to Iranian military
The U.S. Treasury Department imposed sanctions Tuesday on 10 individuals and companies accused of helping Iran's military logistics agency acquire weapons and electronics.
The targets include people based in Iran, Beijing, Hong Kong and Pakistan.
The sanctions are part of a Trump administration initiative called Operation Economic Outcast, aimed at pressuring Iran by isolating its government and economy.
"Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Trump "trapped in a quagmire" when it comes to war, Iran security chief says
President Trump is stuck when it comes to deciding between further war and negotiations, according to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's influential Supreme National Security Council.
"We stated our conditions, but Trump is incapable of decision-making," Rezaei said Tuesday during a meeting with Azerbaijan's deputy prime minister, Shahin Mustafayev. "Trump is trapped in a quagmire where he can neither negotiate nor fight."
Multiple Iranian officials have said they are waiting for a response on the proposal made during last week's U.N. General Assembly, however, Mr. Trump already dismissed the plan on Saturday.
"Our plan, which became known as the seven-point plan, was conveyed to the Americans through the Qatari intermediary," Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters in New York on Monday. "Despite the things that the American president and others said, I said that we are waiting for an official response from America through the intermediary."
Rezaei singled out the strict sanctions on airlines that went into place last week, calling them an "air blockade," as a sign of "desperation."
Iraq begins importing gasoline via Syrian port to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz
Iraqi fuel trucks loaded gasoline at a Syrian port on Tuesday in a bid to meet surging energy demand as the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed and mediators work with Iran and the United States to end the war.
The disruption of the strait has sent shock waves through the global economy, prompting countries to scramble for alternatives and sending fuel prices soaring. A fifth of the world's traded oil and gas transited through the narrow waterway before the war.
Syria, under interim president Ahmad al-Sharaa, who ousted longtime leader Bashar Assad in December 2024, has seized the opportunity to bolster the country's economy by providing an alternative route through the Baniyas port. Markets including the United States and Europe have been using the port.
Iraq has been exporting oil to foreign markets for months by trucking it through Baniyas as a workaround to the closure of Hormuz. Now, through a three-month agreement between the two, Iraq has begun importing gasoline via Syria; the first shipment to Iraq arrived at the port on Thursday.
U.S. sanctions target Iran's military supply chain as status of talks remains uncertain
The U.S. on Tuesday targeted people and firms around the globe that it has accused of being financial facilitators or enablers of Iran's military supply chain, as the Trump administration pushes forward with economic warfare against Tehran at a time when renewed diplomacy between the two countries remains uncertain.
The latest action by the Treasury Department is part of the administration's Operation Economic Outcast campaign, which is aimed at severing "critical financial lifelines" for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government.
"Treasury will not tolerate any support to the regime and will continue to identify, expose, and isolate Iran's enablers," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.
Ten individuals and entities based in Iran, Hong Kong and Pakistan were sanctioned for allegedly procuring weapons and weapon components for Iran's defense ministry as it fights its now seven-month war against the U.S.
U.S. officials have said they want to disrupt Iran's defense systems and further degrade the government's ability to reconstitute its weapons program. The aim of the latest sanctions includes increasing the costs for the people and companies that have assisted Iran's military procurement efforts.
Turkey seizes jet from Iran's Caspian Airlines over unpaid debt after passengers had already boarded
Turkish authorities have seized a plane belonging to Iran's Caspian Airlines at Istanbul Airport, an official said Tuesday, with Turkish and Iranian media linking it to an unpaid $3.4 million debt.
The seizure took place on Monday after passengers had boarded the Boeing 737, which was waiting to take off when officials detained it on the basis of a court-issued seizure order, Turkey's state news agency Anadolu said.
The reports did not mention the recently imposed U.S. sanctions against Iranian airlines as Washington seeks to economically isolate the Islamic Republic.
In a written response to AFP, a Turkish government official confirmed the move, saying it was linked to "a commercial dispute" but did not give further details.
"We can confirm that a Caspian Airlines aircraft at Istanbul Airport was subject to an enforcement measure pursuant to a decision by the competent authorities. The matter arises from a commercial dispute," he said, asking not to be identified.
In a statement quoted by Iranian state television, Caspian Airlines said it had encountered "temporary operational restrictions regarding one of its Boeing aircraft due to an administrative issue in Turkey."
The report said passengers were forced to disembark but the airline had taken "administrative" steps with regard to a debt for "Istanbul Airport services."
It said the plane would return to Iran on Tuesday.
Stocks hold steady as oil prices ease slightly
Stocks held steady on Wall Street Tuesday as falling oil prices and stable Treasury yields took some pressure off the market.
The S&P 500 was mostly unchanged. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 173 points, or 0.4%, as of 10:37 a.m. Eastern time. The Nasdaq composite rose 0.2%.
The majority of stocks within the S&P 500 index lost ground, but several big technology companies helped offset those losses. Nvidia rose 0.8% and Broadcom rose 3.3%. They are among the most valuable companies on Wall Street and those hefty market values give them greater influence over the broader market's direction.
Stocks have been under pressure as oil prices swing sharply as the U.S. war with Iran drags on, helping to push Treasury yields to their highest levels in two decades.
The price of Brent crude oil in the most actively traded part of the oil market fell 1.5% to $96.41 a barrel. It briefly climbed above $100 on Monday before prices eased a bit, but they are still well above the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February.
Mediators continued to work with the United States and Iran on reaching a deal to end the fighting and open the Strait of Hormuz. U.S. President Donald Trump over the weekend rejected an offer from Tehran to reopen the key waterway.
Overall, rising oil prices have been fueling a jump in Treasury yields. Higher yields threaten to slow economic growth by making borrowing more expensive for individuals and businesses. They can also hurt prices for stocks, especially those seen as expensive, including many technology companies that have soared because of the frenzy around AI technology.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 5.25% from 5.24% late Monday, near its highest level since 2007, before the financial crisis and Great Recession sent yields toward zero.
Yemen health system at "breaking point," World Health Organization warns as cholera spreads
The escalating fighting in Yemen is pushing the country's health system to "breaking point," the World Health Organization said Tuesday, warning that diseases like cholera were already circulating widely.
A renewed ground campaign waged by the Iran-backed Houthis against Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces has left hundreds dead and is deepening the country's humanitarian crisis, with at least 145,000 people displaced this month alone, United Nations figures show.
The impoverished country's health system - already weakened by over a decade of civil war - is on the brink.
"Yemen's latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point," warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region, according to the AFP news agency.
"Nine health facilities or assets have now been damaged, put out of service, closed or directly attacked" in the hard-hit areas of Taiz, Lahj and Hodeidah, Heinzelmann said.
Even before the latest escalation, only around 60% of Yemen's health facilities were fully functional, Heinzelmann added, and the country had been facing high malnutrition and outbreaks of diseases including cholera.
CBS/AFP
U.N. envoy meets Houthi negotiators in bid to halt spiraling violence in Yemen
The U.N. envoy for Yemen said Tuesday that he had met with Houthi negotiators over the weekend in an effort to avert further escalation in Yemen, amid fierce battles on the country's west coast between the Iran-backed Houthi rebels and fragmented Saudi-supported government forces.
The renewed violence, which has killed hundreds and displaced tens of thousands, is the latest twist in Yemen's conflict, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, forcing the country's Western- and Saudi-backed government to settle into exile in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia entered the war a year later, leading a multinational coalition in support of the government forces.
In an interview with The Associated Press in Cairo, Hans Grundberg said his meeting in Oman with the Houthis' chief negotiator, Mohammed Abdul-Salam, aimed to look for ways "to avoid seeing the current escalation go even further."
He also held talks in Saudi Arabia with representatives of Yemen's internationally recognized government and other regional powers, including Saudi officials. Saudi Arabia has been the main target of the Houthis' latest escalation, which Grundberg described as "unprecedented" and "dramatic."
Grundberg said the instability in the region, and the "influence of regional parties, including Iran, and also other neighbors to Yemen," has also impacted the course of the Yemen conflict.
CBS/AP
"Iranian order" in Strait of Hormuz is irreversible, says army spokesman
Iranian Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Amir Akrami-Nia said Tuesday that what he described as the new "Iranian order" in the Strait of Hormuz was irreversible.
Speaking at a public gathering in Tehran, Akrami-Nia said Iranian forces would prevent the country's adversaries from using the strategic waterway the way they did in the past.
"With power and determination, we assure you, dear people, that your children are standing in the middle of the Strait of Hormuz, as the greatest achievement of this war, and they will never allow the enemy to exploit this strait as it did in the past," he said, in remarks relayed by the Telegram channel of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps. "The strait is an Iranian strait. An Iranian order has been established over it, and this order is irreversible."
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said he expects a formal response Tuesday from the U.S. to Tehran's latest proposal for a ceasefire, which includes a plan for the phased reopening of the strait to commercial vessels.
Netanyahu says "we have indications" enemies will try to attack Israel ahead of elections
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday said there were "indications" that Israel's enemies could try to attack ahead of elections scheduled for the end of October, without giving details.
"We have indications that ahead of the elections our enemies will try to attack us. So ... I am sending you a message: Don't mess with us, not now and not ever. Our long arm will reach you anywhere, anytime," Netanyahu said during a visit to an Israeli air force base, according to a video published by his office.
The U.S. and Israel jointly launched the war against Iran, but Israeli forces have predominantly focused their recent military efforts on the Iran-backed group Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.
Despite a June deal that provides for the gradual withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanon, Israeli forces continue to strike towns in the south of the neighboring country, according to Lebanon's National News Agency.
CBS/AFP
Iran's military urges Americans to take to the street to protest the war
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps urged Americans to take to the streets to rally against President Trump and the U.S. war against Iran, which the powerful paramilitary force again claimed the Trump administration had lost.
Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for Iran's powerful Revolutionary Guard, said such street protests should denounce what he called the U.S. government's war-mongering policies. He said Americans should "revise their decision" about their leaders.
He accused the United States of using Iran's nuclear program as a ruse to "plunder Iran's wealth" and to turn the country "back into a colony.
Vessel struck by projectile while transiting Strait of Hormuz
A vessel was struck by a suspected projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz late Monday, according to a British maritime security agency.
The U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said it received "a third-party report of a vessel struck by a suspected unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, resulting in a fire."
UKMTO said the fire was extinguished and the crew was safe.
While no country has claimed the attack, it is the latest in a series of recurring strikes on vessels transiting or attempting to transit the vital waterway that connects the energy producers of the Persian Gulf with international markets. Tehran has long warned ships to transit the strait only via a route it has approved, and with permission from Iranian authorities.
The U.S. military has also previously struck and disabled ships linked to Iran as part of the ongoing blockade of Iranian ports.
Value of Iran's currency falls to a new low against the dollar
The value of Iran's currency fell to another record low compared to the U.S. dollar Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for a single dollar, in a stark reflection of how the war in the Middle East has steadily eroded the Iranian economy.
The latest decline came just a day after the rial hit its previous record of 2.4 million to the dollar.
CBS/AP
U.S. sanctions on aviation are "bullying," Iran says
Iranian government spokeswoman Fatemeh Mohajerani said Tuesday that U.S. restrictions affecting Iranian flights amounted to "American bullying," adding that Tehran had filed a complaint with international bodies, including the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO).
"U.S. air sanctions are bullying," Mohajerani said at her weekly press conference, adding that Iran was pursuing the matter through legal channels and had submitted a complaint to ICAO.
She said the government was continuing diplomacy and negotiations while preparing for different scenarios, stressing that "diplomacy and defense are two arms of national interests."
Iran says it is not budging on seven-point ceasefire proposal
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi insisted late Monday that Tehran has made no changes to its proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, as Iran awaits a formal U.S. response to the plan via mediators.
Tehran presented the proposal last week, demanding that in exchange for the strait being reopened, the U.S. meets conditions set out in the memorandum of understanding signed in June by Mr. Trump and his Iranian counterpart.
"Our plan, which became known as the seven-point plan, was conveyed to the Americans through the Qatari intermediary," Araghchi told reporters in New York, where he has been for the U.N. General Assembly. "Despite the things that the American president and others said, I said that we are waiting for an official response from America through the intermediary."
Iran threatens to use "new weapon" to defend itself
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Tuesday that it is developing new weapons to defend the Islamic Republic.
"We are constantly designing and upgrading new and existing weapons to defend ourselves," IRGC spokesman Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, without offering any real detail.
"We use all the technologies of the world to build new weapons in order to defend our people and our country, and if necessary, we will use these weapons to defend our country," he said.
Mohebbi said the U.S. had failed to achieve its objectives through military and economic pressure, and predicted that "ultimately, America will be forced to leave the region."
Iran threatens regional infrastructure
Iran's chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Tuesday that if his country's security was not guaranteed, no infrastructure in the region would be safe from attack, state media reported.
"In a region where we cannot sell oil, no one else will sell oil either; or if our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will remain safe," said Ghalibaf, who is also Iran's parliament speaker, according to video released by state TV.
Iran says it expects an answer today from U.S. on proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he expected a formal answer on Tuesday from the United States to Tehran's proposal to open the Strait of Hormuz, state media reported.
Qatari intermediaries "presented ideas, and we discussed them; they are set to raise the matter with the American side once more, after which the final U.S. response will be conveyed to us," Araghchi said late Monday.
Iran's top diplomat, who is in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, said "the Qataris hope this will be done by tomorrow."
On Iran talks, Trump says "I offered them NOTHING"
President Trump denied that he has offered to relieve Iran of some sanctions and unfreeze its funds, writing on Truth Social: "I offered them NOTHING!"
The president was reacting to an Axios story that said Mr. Trump is open to granting sanctions relief in exchange for progress on Iran's nuclear program.
A U.S. official also told CBS News on Monday that Mr. Trump is willing to grant Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if progress is made on the nuclear issue.
Trump confirms U.S. spoke to Iranian negotiators through mediators today
President Trump confirmed to reporters that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday.
He did not share any details on the talks, saying, "We're going to win."
CBS News reported earlier Monday that indirect U.S.-Iran talks began in the morning. A U.S. official said Mr. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on Iran's nuclear program, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, and the two sides remain apart on the timing of commitments.
An Iranian diplomatic source told CBS News the primary issue is that the U.S. president does not seem to have a clear position on what he wants from negotiations, making it difficult to move from discussions to a concrete agreement.
Uncertainty about Strait of Hormuz weighs on U.S. bond market
Yields in the U.S. bond market cranked higher Monday and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked U.S. stocks further from their record high.
Monday's rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices, which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide.
The latest turns came after President Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
Gas prices could soar if the U.S. bans diesel exports, economists say
A move by the U.S. to temporarily halt diesel exports amid record-high prices would initially lower costs, but a prolonged ban could drive up domestic gasoline prices, according to Goldman Sachs.
President Trump on Sunday told reporters his administration is "very seriously" considering a ban on diesel exports. Calls to restrict exports of U.S.-refined diesel have picked up in recent weeks, mostly from Republican lawmakers, as a lever they believe will help lower prices. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, and has only eased slightly since then, slipping to $6.45 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA data.
The war with Iran is pushing up oil and gas prices, creating widespread financial strain on U.S. motorists, food delivery drivers and farmers.
Read more here.
Yemen says it launched over 350 strikes against Houthi targets
Yemen's defense ministry said it carried out 356 strikes against Houthi military targets over the past 24 hours, killing or wounding an estimated 476 fighters.
Video posted by the Yemeni military showed strikes on various Houthi positions across several front lines.
Military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nazili said the strikes targeted Houthi command centers, weapons depots, artillery positions, vehicles and other military equipment.
U.S. official: Talks ongoing through mediators, but no deal unless nuclear issue addressed
The U.S. and Iran are continuing to have discussions, viewed as positive and constructive, through mediators, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on nuclear issues, the official said. Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, but the two sides still remain apart on the timing of commitments and who takes which steps first.
The official said the U.S. is skeptical of Iran's promises after it broke the memorandum of understanding by firing on commercial vessels, and is looking for assurances that Iran is serious.
Iranians face arduous journeys as U.S. sanctions ground planes
Flying out of Iran has long required patience in the face of restrictions and delays, but new U.S. sanctions have grounded flights on short notice and left war-weary travelers feeling trapped as they try to leave the country.
Passengers who booked tickets out of Iran to Middle Eastern destinations like the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman and Turkey have faced short-notice cancellations as the latest sanctions bite.
Among those scrambling for a way out is Mitra, a 49-year-old woman who had planned to travel to Paris via Istanbul along with her brother, but who now faces a long journey by road to get to Turkey.
"Some airlines are still selling tickets, but they keep getting canceled. It honestly makes us feel completely trapped," she told an AFP journalist in Paris, using a pseudonym for fear of retribution by authorities.
"When we were told that flights had been suspended, we decided to travel to Istanbul by land instead," she said.
Mitra described paying around $75 to book a flight to the Iranian city of Tabriz, from where she will travel by road for several hours to reach the border.
In Van in Turkey, they will stay at a hotel, because the wait at the border can be long and chaotic.
"At this point, we're just hoping that we can actually get out. They might even close the land border," she fears.
Israel releases on bail U.S.-Palestinian reporter accused of working for Iran
An Israeli court on Monday released on bail a Palestinian American journalist who had been detained for nearly two weeks on charges including working for Iran, her lawyer told the AFP news agency.
An AFP journalist saw Naqaa Hamed, who has contributed to Iran's state-run Press TV, being released at a checkpoint near Jenin in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Hamed's lawyer Khaled Mahajneh told AFP that an Israeli military court released her on bail of 8,000 shekels — about $2,600 — and on condition she comply with future summons for questioning.
Mahajneh said Hamed spent "two weeks of detention under difficult conditions at Damon prison" in the northern Israeli city of Haifa.
The Israeli military arrested Hamed on Sept. 15 at a checkpoint near Bethlehem as she was returning from a reporting assignment for Turkish broadcaster TRT, according to her family and a journalist who was accompanying her at the time.
Press TV, which is owned by the Iranian state, reported on her arrest and release and described her as its West Bank correspondent.
Colleagues said Hamed, who holds U.S. citizenship, had stopped working with Press TV about a month earlier and had become a freelance journalist.
The Israeli government considers Press TV a propaganda arm of Iran's government.
Israel is currently holding 36 journalists in its prisons, according to the Palestinian Prisoners' Club, an NGO working for prisoners' rights.
Rising oil prices push U.S. stock values down as Trump rejects Iran's latest offer
Rising oil prices are knocking the U.S. stock market further from its record high on Monday, while building pressure even higher within the U.S. bond market.
The S&P 500 fell 0.8% and gave back most of its gains from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 372 points, or 0.7%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1% lower.
Most of the U.S. stock market sank under the weight of a 2.8% rise for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude oil to $100.19 per barrel. That overshadowed a gain for Wall Street's most influential stock, Nvidia, after it announced a historic funneling of cash to its investors through a buyback of its shares.
Oil prices have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
"I'd like to make a deal, too," Mr. Trump said Saturday. "But that deal would not be acceptable."
Brent climbed above $101 per barrel Monday morning, before the U.S. stock market opened for trading, but it pared its gains as U.S. officials said mediators were still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end the fighting and open the strait.
For all its ups and downs, a barrel of Brent remains much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. That has helped worsen inflation, and the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is up to nearly $4.48 from $3.13 a year ago, according to AAA.
Iranian foreign minister to meet mediators in New York over potential renewal of talks with U.S.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is scheduled to meet mediators in New York on Monday morning to discuss the latest proposals and efforts to revive negotiations with the United States, Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency reported.
According to ISNA, Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of a deal to end the war, in exchange for the release of Iranian funds and assets that Tehran says have been unlawfully blocked.
The proposal was conveyed to the U.S. through mediators in New York. Although President Trump rejected the offer over the weekend, Iranian officials say indirect contacts and mediation efforts continue.
Araghchi said Iran is awaiting a response via the mediators before deciding its next steps. He reiterated that any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz would depend on Iran's conditions being met, saying Tehran would not back down from its conditions.
"We are waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators and we will make a decision based on that," ISNA quoted Araghchi as saying.
No representatives from the U.S. side will be attending Monday's meeting, the report said.

"We are waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators and we will make a decision based on that," ISNA quoted Araghchi as saying.
No representatives from the U.S. side will be attending Monday's meeting, the report said.
U.K. police release on bail 5 men arrested near air base used by U.S. for Iran strikes
British counter terror police released on bail five British men arrested over the weekend near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran.
Metropolitan Police Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said the men were being released following "extensive interviews," adding that the investigation was not over and they remained "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."
Referring to reports that British authorities were investigating a possible link to Iran, he said: "I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident."
"At this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation … be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iran said Monday that it "categorically denies" any involvement in the incident.
Iran "categorically rejects" involvement in suspected terror plot on military base hosting U.S. aircraft
Iran "categorically rejects" claims that it was involved in a suspected terror plot on a British military base hosting U.S. aircraft, its embassy in London said Monday.
British counterterrorism police were leading an investigation Monday after five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act in an English village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers.
The Associated Press reported that British authorities are investigating the possibility of a link between Iran and the arrests near RAF Fairford, but that as of Monday there had been no conclusions reached about whether the apparent plot against the base could have been state-backed.
This year, groups with purported links to Iran have carried out several attacks on U.K. soil, primarily targeting the Jewish community in north London.
U.S. and Iran expected to continue talking this week through mediators, official tells Reuters
The U.S. and Iran are expected to have separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, an official with knowledge of the negotiations told the Reuters news agency.
With Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the U.S., as well as Qatari mediators, the talks are set to focus on an updated version of the seven-day proposal Iran gave to U.S. counterparts last week during the United Nations General Assembly, the official told Reuters.
President Trump said Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume in the coming days, a day after he rejected a new proposal put forward by Tehran last week for a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Saudi Arabia's strategic East-West Crude Oil Pipeline operational again, Bloomberg says
Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil using its crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after drone strikes earlier this month forced it shut, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter quoted by Bloomberg.
Saudi Arabia had been using the pipeline to transport oil from its eastern production hubs to its Red Sea ports for export — a vital alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted by the U.S.-Iran war.
The pipeline was shut down earlier this month after a series of drone attacks that Saudi authorities blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
The state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco, which operates the kingdom's oil infrastructure, tested the pipeline last week and has now resumed overseas shipments via the Red Sea route, a source familiar with the operation told Bloomberg.
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have vowed to impose a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports and against Saudi ships, and they have targeted several vessels in the region.
Iran lodges complaint with U.N. over U.S. sanctions on its aviation industry
Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.
The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.
As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.
"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
CBS/AFP
Ayatollah Khamenei says U.S. forces will soon be pushed back
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah — who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began — said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
Value of Iran's currency falls to all-time low against the dollar
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center.
Iran's U.N. delegation has no plans to negotiate directly with the U.S.
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side ... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.
CBS/AFP
British police investigating possible Iranian links to suspected terrorist plot against U.K. air base used by U.S.
U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Fairford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.
Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.
President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.
"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."
Iran says it is ready for either diplomacy, or a return to fighting as war reaches 7-month mark
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.
President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week
President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz over seven days, but Mr. Trump asserted that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly."
"They overplayed their hand," Mr. Trump told Axios.
The president said resuming strikes on Iran was not off the table, adding: "I am always thinking about it."
CBS/AFP
Sen. Kennedy says Iran's plan was "not a serious offer"
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said Iran's proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks was "not a serious offer."
"The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down," Kennedy said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"We need to continue doing what we're doing — the sanctions, the blockade," said Kennedy.
"Now there's just one problem: The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil. And oil's in everything, including gasoline, and it's painful as hell," he said, adding: "We've got to either figure out a way to settle this thing, to get the strait open, or to escalate."
Kennedy said he would not support sending U.S. ground troops into Iran, however.
results.summary:
Tensions between the United States and Iran remain high as the Trump administration imposes new sanctions while indirect negotiations regarding a potential ceasefire and the Strait of Hormuz continue.

### Key Points
- The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned 10 individuals and companies for allegedly facilitating Iran's military logistics and weapons procurement.
- Iran’s currency, the rial, hit a record low of 2.5 million per dollar as the seven-month conflict continues to erode the nation's economy.
- Iraq has begun importing gasoline through a Syrian port to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz, which remains a critical bottleneck for global energy supplies.
- President Trump rejected Iran's recent seven-day ceasefire proposal, though he confirmed that indirect communication between the two nations is ongoing via mediators.
- The World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system is at a "breaking point" due to escalating violence involving Iran-backed Houthi forces.

### Why it Matters
The ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to drive global oil price volatility, placing significant inflationary pressure on the U.S. economy and international markets. As diplomatic efforts remain stalled, the combination of economic sanctions and military posturing increases the risk of further regional instability and prolonged energy supply disruptions.
